A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same PRO research. Their main text, equations, tables, figures, references, and complete appendices are readable and can be matched despite supplementary-section reorganization.

before.justification: v1 reports original depth-estimation comparisons, component and overlap ablations, and an appendix experiment comparing frequency fusion with convolutional fusion.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds experiments with alternative base models, BFM transfer, inference patch counts, and diagonal consistency training.

M1.justification: The residual refinement architecture, four-patch GPCT, BFM, frequency fusion, and losses are retained. Explicit patch arguments in ROI operations and additional indices clarify existing notation. Newly documented preprocessing does not establish a change to the underlying procedure.

E1.justification: Both versions use UnrealStereo4K for training and evaluate on Booster, ETH3D, Middlebury 2014, NuScenes, DIS-5K, UHRSD, and internet images. UHRSD and internet examples already appear in v1's appendix. Alternative base models and patch counts change configurations within retained coverage.

E2.justification: The main comparison methods remain unchanged. New supplementary comparisons evaluate standalone MiDaS v3.1 and DepthAnythingV1 alongside their refinement variants, BFM-trained PatchFusion and PatchRefiner, and a two-patch diagonal-consistency control (Tables 5, 6, and 8). These extend the comparisons without replacing the original baseline families.

E3.justification: Supplement A adds substantial experimental controls: retraining with two alternative base models, enabling BFM in other architectures, testing 3×3/4×4/5×5 inference grids, and comparing diagonal regularization with GPCT. Existing primary evaluation settings remain. Section 4.4 also changes the stated overlap interpretation from its shorter side to a square-region size; this does not establish that earlier experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: v2 adds analyses of base-model generality and transparent-object failure, BFM transfer to other methods, patch-count sensitivity, and GPCT versus diagonal consistency (Supplement A, Tables 5–8 and Figures 6–7). The original component, overlap-size, and frequency-fusion ablations are retained; v1's FFM Table 5 becomes v2's Table 9.

E5.justification: Neither version reports experimental seed counts, repeated-run uncertainty, confidence intervals, or statistical tests. The added experiments continue the existing point-estimate reporting practice.

E6.justification: Tables 1–4 and the relocated FFM results are numerically unchanged, but v2 adds substantial results in Tables 5–8. For example, diagonal consistency has CE 0.075 versus GPCT's 0.049, while achieving better D3R, 0.0787 versus 0.0803. Table 7 reports DIS boundary recall of 0.125, 0.156, and 0.162 for 3×3, 4×4, and 5×5 grids. These are additional comparisons, not revised headline scores.

T1.justification: Equations 1–10 retain the same refinement, consistency, masking, and frequency-fusion operations. Explicit ROI patch arguments and patch indices are equivalent notation changes. No new assumptions, theorems, proofs, or substantive derivations are introduced.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain GPCT for consistent single-pass patch refinement, BFM for avoiding synthetic-label bias, strong zero-shot depth performance, and approximately 12× faster inference than PatchRefiner with 177 patches. The added experiments support the existing generality claim rather than redefine it.

C2.justification: Supplement A newly explains that poor transparent-object predictions from DA1 can undermine refinement: DA1-based PRO has Booster AbsRel 0.0500 versus unrefined DA1's 0.0482. It also interprets the BFM transfer experiments as evidence of broader applicability and patch-count variation as a speed/detail adjustment available without retraining.

D1.justification: New Supplement C fills important implementation gaps by specifying rejection of samples with more than 50% unreliable pixels, native-resolution crop and patch geometry, overlap scaling, and assembly into a 2072×2072 depth map followed by bilinear upsampling. Supplement A also states that replacing the base model requires retraining. These are newly disclosed details, not demonstrated changes to previously run experiments.

R1.justification: The same 49 cited works and substantive positioning relative to previous depth-estimation methods are retained. The new experiments use already cited methods; added citation markers and changed reference back-links do not expand the literature coverage.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, and portions of the method receive extensive language editing and paragraph rewriting. The appendix is reorganized into supplementary Sections A–D, with dedicated experiment and implementation sections, while notation, terminology, and captions are clarified throughout.

P2.justification: v2 adds four supplementary tables and two qualitative figures, substantially expanding the displayed experimental evidence. It places the retained FFM table beside its architecture discussion and updates diagram labels. The original qualitative panels are retained and renumbered, including v1 Figures 7–10 becoming v2 Figures 9–12.

improvement.justification: v1's broad integration claim was tested principally with DA2, and its GPCT ablation lacked a direct diagonal-consistency control. v2 addresses both gaps through alternative-base experiments and a targeted comparison, while reporting a DA1 failure case and metric-dependent tradeoffs. The newly specified sample filtering and reconstruction steps also materially improve reproducibility. Together these changes substantially strengthen the paper's validation and clarify applicability, despite unchanged headline results.
